name: How Broker Consensus Actually Works (And Why It's Broken)
author: Anonymous (believed active broker, the Gray Zone/Narrows corridor, GLMZ-Central)
description: A practitioner's guide to the Signal Network's actual mechanics, written anonymously by a broker operating in the Gray Zone/Narrows corridor. Circulated through physical drop channels sometime in late 2198, this document describes the gap between the stated consensus model of broker tier-assignment and the reality of clique dynamics, personal grievances, and reputation-laundering that governs how freelancers actually move through the system. Considered candid to the point of professional risk for its author.
body:
I'm writing this because someone asked me to explain how the Signal Network works, and I spent twenty minutes giving them the standard answer — vouching chains, Dead Drop aggregation, active broker consensus — and I watched their face go completely flat. They'd done everything right and gotten nowhere for eight months. The standard answer wasn't wrong. It just wasn't true.

So here is the true version, as best as I can give it without burning myself entirely.

---

**THE THEORY**

You already know this part, but I'll state it so we have something to compare against.

The Signal Network has no central authority. Freelancer tier designations emerge from broker consensus: multiple active brokers reviewing Dead Drop tokens, vouching chains, and job outcomes, arriving at rough agreement about whether someone is C, B, A, or S. Ghost tier is its own thing and I'm not going to touch it here. The whole model is supposed to be self-correcting — bad actors lose vouches, good performers accumulate them, and no single broker can crown someone or bury them unilaterally.

That is the theory. It is correct in the same way that a building's architectural drawings are correct: accurate about structure, silent about the water damage in the east stairwell.

---

**HOW IT ACTUALLY WORKS**

Brokers talk to other brokers. That's the mechanism. Everything flows from that.

The problem is that we don't all talk to each other. We talk to the people we trust, which means the people we've worked with successfully, which means the people in our corridor, our era, our deal history. I have four brokers I communicate with regularly. Maybe eight I'd reach out to for a second opinion on something unusual. There are probably sixty active brokers operating in the GLMZ-Central and Narrows corridor alone. Most of them are people I have nodded at, at best.

So when I'm evaluating whether to accept a vouch or upgrade my assessment of a freelancer, I'm drawing on a network that represents maybe 15% of the broker ecosystem at any given time. And so is everyone else. We're not running a consensus model. We're running a set of overlapping cliques that occasionally agree with each other.

This matters because cliques have histories. Raina Beckett and the group she works with — I don't mean this as an insult, it's just geography — they run the Gray Zone-lower circuit and they have not had a real conversation with the Narrows-upper group since the Kovacs job in 2194. You don't know what the Kovacs job was and I'm not going to tell you. The point is: a freelancer who builds their reputation entirely through the Gray Zone-lower vouches is functionally invisible to half the Narrows-upper broker community, regardless of how solid their Dead Drops are. They can't cross that line without someone physically bridging it, and bridging costs the broker social capital they may not want to spend.

Tier movement — especially C to B, which is where most people die waiting — isn't a vote. It's a conversation that either happens or doesn't. And whether it happens depends on whether any broker with cross-clique relationships thinks a freelancer is worth the social effort of advocacy.

---

**THE DEAD DROP PROBLEM**

Dead Drops are supposed to be the objective layer. Physical tokens, standardized enough that brokers can aggregate them without personal interpretation. A freelancer runs a job, the client or crew leaves a token at an established drop point, the broker who holds that route collects and logs it.

Here is what actually happens with Dead Drop data:

First, not all drops are checked with the same frequency. Routes through contested zones, or drops that require physical access to inconvenient locations, go cold for weeks at a time. Tokens rot, get lifted by opportunists, or just sit there. A freelancer who completed three solid jobs in the Sublevel 9 corridor in 2197 may have zero Drop record because the broker holding that route stopped servicing it after a security sweep.

Second, aggregation is manual and interpretive. There is no automated system here. A broker reads physical tokens and decides what they mean. Tokens are not signed. A token that says a freelancer did a clean extraction could mean they did a clean extraction. It could also mean a client wanted to look like the extraction went clean for reasons of their own. Experienced brokers get good at triangulating between tokens and other information. Less experienced brokers, or brokers who are busy, or brokers who already have an opinion — they read what confirms what they already think.

---

**WHY PROMOTION ISN'T ALWAYS MERIT**

Two kinds of freelancers move fast through the tiers. The first kind are genuinely exceptional and got lucky enough to work jobs that put them in front of the right brokers during a window when those brokers were paying attention and had no conflicts of interest. This is rare.

The second kind have a sponsor. Not a formal sponsor — nothing is formal — but a broker who decides that advocating for this particular freelancer is worth the political effort. This happens for a lot of reasons that are not merit. Sometimes it's because the freelancer did a job that saved someone the broker cares about. Sometimes it's because the broker is building their own network and needs to seed it with loyalists. Sometimes it's because the freelancer is dating someone. I'm not going to pretend that doesn't happen. It happens.

Brokering a promotion requires a broker to go to their contacts and say: this person is worth the upgrade. That statement puts the broker's credibility on the line. Brokers are more likely to do this for people they feel certain about, and certainty is easier when there's a personal relationship. That's just how humans work. The network doesn't fix it.

---

**WHY DEMOTION IS NEARLY IMPOSSIBLE**

This is the part nobody talks about.

Demoting a freelancer means a broker has to say, publicly in the broker network: I endorsed someone who turned out to be a problem. Or: I failed to catch that someone I vouched through was compromised.

Almost no broker will do this voluntarily. The vouch chain runs backward through you. If you pushed someone to B tier and they burned a client, walking that back means admitting you misjudged them. Most brokers would rather quietly stop routing work to that freelancer and let the silence do the work. Which means the freelancer stays technically tier-ranked but functionally dry — no jobs coming through — and no one tells them why, and no one tells other brokers why, because that would require the original broker to explain their error.

This is how problem freelancers persist in the system. Not through conspiracy. Through individual brokers protecting their own assessment history.

---

**THE TWO MOST COMMON WAYS TO GAME IT**

The first is token seeding: arranging for Dead Drops to receive favorable tokens from clients who didn't actually have a clean experience, or for jobs that weren't as described. This works in the short term because brokers are busy and no one audits drops systematically. It stops working when a broker with genuine contacts in the corridor starts comparing notes and the seeded tokens don't match what anyone remembers.

The second is clique shopping: finding a broker cluster that doesn't communicate with the cluster handling your actual job history, presenting a curated story to the new group, and building a parallel reputation. This can work for a surprisingly long time in a fragmented network. It collapses the first time someone from both clusters ends up in the same room.

I've watched both of these run for twelve, eighteen months before someone caught the thread. I've also watched people try both and get caught in six weeks. The network is inconsistent. That's not a feature or a bug. That's just what it is.

---

None of this means the Signal Network doesn't work. It works better than nothing, which is what existed before it and what still exists in the zones where it hasn't taken hold. The people it elevates are more often competent than not. The people it filters out often deserved filtering.

But if you're a freelancer who's been doing solid work for a year and you're still C tier, the answer is probably not that the system hasn't noticed you yet. The answer is that the right broker hasn't had a reason to care.

Figure out who that is. Then figure out how to give them a reason.

That's the actual guide.
